title: Financial Management
method: P10 carries no acceptance criteria at all — see finding P10-F1 — so each requirement was judged against its own statement, which is specific enough to serve as one. The 240 requirements factor exactly: 16 subjects by 15 aspects, every aspect appearing once per subject. A requirement is verified only where the aspect holds AND the subject it applies to exists. Aspects are assessed platform-wide with per-subject exceptions recorded, because effective dating, period control and export are platform properties rather than per-subject ones.

findings.title: 797 requirements across five phases carry no acceptance criteria
findings.detail: P04, P06, P07, P08 and P10 — 797 of the register's 9,475 requirements — have an empty acceptance_criteria column. P10's requirement statements are specific and well formed, better than the templated statements elsewhere in the register; they simply have no criteria attached.
findings.why_it_matters: Verification here means somebody read a requirement's acceptance criteria and confirmed a named test asserts it. For 8.4% of the register that method cannot run as defined. It is a property of the requirements spine rather than of this codebase, and it bounds how much of the register can ever be verified rather than merely traced.
findings.why_not_resolved: Writing the missing criteria and then judging against them would be marking my own homework, and the traceability system exists precisely to keep derived work and confirmed work apart. P10 was instead judged against the requirement statements themselves, which is defensible because they are specific, and this verdict records that the criteria came from the statement rather than from the register. The remaining four phases are noted for whoever owns the spine.

findings.title: Job cost had no cutoff, so a reported figure could change retroactively
findings.detail: `project_costs` carries a `cost_date` and `ap_invoices` an `invoice_date`, and nothing could close a period. A cost dated last March could be posted today, changing a job cost figure already reported to an owner, a bank or a bonding company.
findings.why_it_matters: It is the same family as the schedule float, the plan terms and the claim deadline — a number that moved after somebody acted on it — but retroactive, which is worse: the report was right when it was produced and is wrong now, and nothing says which.
findings.resolution: Migration 0034 adds `financial_periods` with a non-overlapping date range per company, a close that refuses to run over a pay application still in draft or submitted, and a reopen that requires an attributed reason. `app.enforce_open_period` refuses a posting into a closed period and equally refuses moving an existing posting out of one, because the period total would change after it was reported either way. A company that has defined no periods is not running a close and is left alone. 20 database tests.

findings.title: There is no general ledger, and this phase is largely about one
findings.detail: No chart of accounts, no journal entry, no fiscal calendar beyond the periods just added, no trial balance, no posting, no consolidation. A search of the entire schema and source tree for any of these returns nothing. What exists is construction operational finance: schedule of values, AIA pay applications with certified immutability, AP invoices with three-way match, job cost, committed cost and retainage.
findings.why_it_matters: Six of the sixteen subjects in this phase — General Ledger, Cash & Treasury, Tax & Regulatory Finance, Revenue Recognition, AI Financial Intelligence, and most of Financial Core & Governance — have no implementation to judge. Stating that plainly is more useful than a partial verdict that implies something is there.
findings.why_not_resolved: A general ledger is a subsystem, not a gap. It also may not belong here: the platform integrates with accounting systems through its API and payroll export rather than replacing them, and building a half-ledger would be worse than having none — it would invite people to report from it. That is a product decision, not a build decision, and it is recorded here for whoever makes it.

aspects.name: tenant-scoped records
aspects.evidence: Every financial table carries company_id with row level security enabled and forced, policies generated by two audited helpers rather than written by hand, and app.enforce_tenant_parent refusing a child row attached to a parent owned by another company. 460 database tests run against real PostgreSQL with two provisioned companies.

aspects.name: configurable approval thresholds and routing
aspects.gap: Approval tiers exist and, since migration 0033, configurable per-company signing thresholds govern change orders, contracts and claim settlements. Nothing of the kind exists for financial records: a pay application is approved by anyone holding finance.write regardless of its value, and there is no routing — no sequence of approvers, no delegation, no escalation.

aspects.match: shall create an immutable audit event
aspects.name: immutable audit event for every action
aspects.gap: Create, update and delete are captured on every financial table by an append-only ledger recording prior and new state, and approve and post appear within it as updates. Export does not: nothing records that data left the platform, which is one of the seven actions this aspect names and the one an auditor asks about first. Reverse is not modeled as an action at all, because there is nothing to reverse.

aspects.name: role-based and attribute-based access control
aspects.evidence: Role-based: named roles carry explicit permission arrays and an approval tier, checked by app.has_permission with wildcards honored only as the whole grant. Attribute-based: a membership's project_scope narrows a user to named projects, every policy predicates on the row's own company_id, and contracts are readable under finance.read while written under estimates.approve, so a role can draft one without seeing the portfolio's financial position.

aspects.name: effective dating, versioning and historical reconstruction
aspects.gap: Library rates carry effective dating and row history, estimates carry versions with pinned library snapshots, and plans now carry versions. No financial record does: a pay application, a job cost and a payable each have one current state and no history beyond the audit ledger, so a prior period cannot be reconstructed as it stood.

aspects.name: source-to-ledger balance validation
aspects.gap: There is no ledger to balance to. Individual arithmetic is defended — a pay application cannot bill more than the contract sum plus approved changes, a work order's total is generated from its parts, an achieved production rate is a generated column — but no double entry exists and nothing can be unbalanced.

aspects.name: configurable statuses and state transitions
aspects.gap: Statuses are explicit and constrained, and transitions are enforced — a pay application cannot leave draft without a submission timestamp, a claim cannot advance past potential without a notice date, an executed change order cannot move back. None of it is configurable: the states and the transitions are in the schema, and a company cannot add a review step of its own.

aspects.name: governed APIs and event notifications
aspects.gap: Nine versioned endpoints sit behind a pure authorization function with one error shape, scoped API keys stored only as a hash, and an OpenAPI specification generated from the route table with drift failing the build — the API half is genuinely governed. The event half does not exist: there are no outbound webhooks and no event stream, so nothing outside the platform can be notified that a financial record changed.

aspects.name: dashboards, drill-downs and exportable reports
aspects.gap: Dashboards and drill-downs exist as screens over five reporting views, each with security_invoker so a view can never become the way around row level security. Export does not exist anywhere in the platform: no export permission, no export path, and nothing that records an export having happened — the same absence P28 recorded.

aspects.name: attachments, notes, evidence and source-document lineage
aspects.gap: Documents are versioned with supersession and a claim's citations are now integrity-checked against them. No financial record links to a document: an AP invoice cannot carry the invoice image it was entered from, and a pay application cannot carry the signed certificate. Lineage from a source document to a financial figure therefore stops at the operational record.

aspects.name: multi-company and intercompany processing
aspects.gap: Multi-company is the platform's foundation: companies, enterprise groups, corporate standard libraries with company overrides, and a plan limit on how many companies a subscription carries. Intercompany processing is absent — nothing records a transaction between two companies in a group, and there is no elimination or reconciliation between them.

aspects.name: configurable accounting dimensions
aspects.gap: The dimensions this aspect names mostly exist as columns: company, project, cost code, equipment, customer and vendor all appear on the records they belong to, and divisions and offices exist above the project. They are fixed columns rather than dimensions: a company cannot add one, and nothing lets a figure be sliced by a dimension the schema did not anticipate.

aspects.name: duplicate, anomaly and policy-exception detection
aspects.gap: Three-way match compares an invoice against its purchase order and delivery and refuses a mismatch, which is one policy exception detected well. Nothing detects a duplicate invoice, an anomalous cost, a missing required field on an otherwise valid record, or a policy exception of any other kind.

aspects.name: period controls, cutoff validation and posting-date governance
aspects.evidence: Migration 0034: non-overlapping accounting periods per company, enforced by an exclusion constraint so the closed-or-open answer never depends on which row was read first. Closing refuses to run over a pay application still in draft or submitted, and records who closed it and when; reopening requires an attributed reason. Postings into a closed period are refused, and so is moving an existing posting out of one, because the period total would change after it was reported either way. A company that has defined no periods is left alone rather than having a close invented for it. 20 tests.

aspects.name: traceability from operational transaction to financial statement
aspects.gap: The operational half of this chain is strong and tested: measured field production ties to a task, the task to the estimate line it was budgeted from, the line to the library rows that priced it through a snapshot, and cost to the same task. The financial half does not exist — there is no financial statement for anything to have an impact on.

Financial Core & Governance.note: Accounting periods now exist and are governed. A fiscal calendar beyond them, a chart of accounts, entities below the company, and currency handling beyond a column on a price do not.

General Ledger.note: No journal entry, no chart of accounts, no trial balance, no posting, no consolidation, no close beyond the period cutoff.

Accounts Payable.note: AP invoices with three-way match against purchase order and delivery, vendor records, and now a posting-date cutoff.

Accounts Receivable.note: Pay applications bill the owner and record what was paid against them. There is no receivable of its own: no customer invoice separate from the pay application, no aging, no receipt application, no collections.

Job Cost & WIP.note: Cost by type and cost code against a project and a task, committed cost from purchase orders, budget from the awarded estimate, and a work-in-progress reporting view.

Construction Billing.note: Schedule of values, AIA G702 pay applications with cumulative-to-date arithmetic, retainage at the contract percentage, and a certified application that cannot be edited.

Payroll Accounting Integration.note: Time entries carry hours, cost code and project, are approved, and lock once exported to a named payroll batch. Nothing posts payroll to an accounting system or reconciles what came back.

Cash & Treasury.note: No bank account, no cash position, no forecast, no reconciliation, no payment run.

Budgeting & Forecasting.note: A project carries an approved budget and job cost reports against it. There is no forecast: no cost to complete, no estimate at completion, no re-forecast cycle.

Fixed Assets.note: Assets carry acquisition cost, ownership, meter readings and maintenance history, and equipment rates recover ownership cost in an estimate. There is no fixed asset accounting: no depreciation schedule, no book value, no disposal.

Tax & Regulatory Finance.note: Sales tax appears in material cost derivation for estimating. No tax jurisdiction, no filing, no exemption certificate, no regulatory report.

Procurement Finance.note: Purchase orders with committed cost, quote leveling, deliveries, inventory with a transaction ledger, and three-way match into payables.

Revenue Recognition.note: No percentage of completion, no earned revenue, no over- or under-billing calculation, no contract asset or liability.

Integrations & Data Exchange.note: A versioned public API generated from its own route table, scoped API keys, governed connectors, and a payroll batch export.

AI Financial Intelligence.note: The one governed agent reads documents. Nothing applies it to financial data, and under RULE-008 anything that did would propose rather than post.

Security, Audit & Compliance.note: Row level security forced on every financial table, an append-only audit ledger no privilege level can edit, certified pay applications frozen, and the security gates that fail a migration leaving a table open.

Integrations & Data Exchange.A14: not_met — an integration has no posting-dated record of its own for a period to govern.

Security, Audit & Compliance.A14: not_met — audit and access control are not posting-dated.
